en: Sutta Nipāta 3.5 Māghasutta Thus have I heard:
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha on Vulture’s Peak Mountain.
Then the young brahmin Māgha approached the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him.
When they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, he sat down to one side.
As Māgha the young brahmin was sitting to one side, he said this to the Blessed One:
“Master Gotama, I am indeed a giver, a lord of giving, generous, and devoted to the practice of almsgiving;
I seek wealth in accordance with the Dhamma.”
Having sought wealth righteously, with wealth acquired righteously and attained through righteousness,
I give to one, and I give to two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, and ten; I give to twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, and even to a hundred.
“I give, and I give even more.
Master Gotama, by giving in this way and sacrificing in this way, do I produce much merit?
“Indeed, young man, by giving in this way and sacrificing in this way, you produce much merit.”
“Māṇava, whoever is a donor, a master of giving, generous, and devoted to giving;
who seeks wealth righteously;

and having sought wealth righteously, having acquired wealth righteously and obtained it through righteous means, gives to one person …pe… gives to a hundred people, and gives even more—such a person produces much merit.”
Then the young brahmin Māgha addressed the Blessed One in verse:
“I ask Gotama, the one who speaks with wisdom,” (said the young brahmin Māgha).
To one who dwells in a house, clothed in saffron robes, wandering as a mendicant—
whosoever is a householder, a master of giving, devoted to making requests,
seeking merit, and yearning for merit— who offers a sacrifice.
“How does the offering of food and drink given here by another become purified for the one performing the sacrifice?
“The householder who is a master of giving, devoted to the practice of soliciting [others],”
(Māgha, said the Blessed One:
"Seeking merit and desiring merit, one sacrifices;
giving food and drink here to others,"
“May such a one as you, O worthy recipient,
be propitiated. “The householder who is devoted to making requests and is a master of giving,” (thus spoke Māgha the young brahmin).
Seeking merit and desiring merit,
one gives food and drink here to others;
tell me, Blessed One, who are the worthy recipients of offerings.
“To those indeed who wander in the world unattached,
possessing nothing, being whole, and self-controlled—
to them one should offer the sacrificial gift at the proper time.”
That brahmin who, seeking merit, should sacrifice—
those who have severed all fetters and bonds,
who are tamed, liberated, free from affliction, and without longing;
At the proper time, a brahmin seeking merit who would sacrifice should offer the sacrificial oblation to them—
those who are completely liberated from all fetters.
Their teeth are worn away, they are free from affliction and devoid of desire;
at the proper time, one should offer the sacrificial oblation to them—
any brahmin who seeks merit should perform sacrifice unto them.
Having abandoned lust, hatred, and delusion,
those whose taints are destroyed have lived the holy life;
at the proper time, one should offer sacrificial food to them.
That brahmin who, seeking merit,
should sacrifice to those in whom neither deceit nor pride dwells—
those whose taints are destroyed and who have lived the holy life.
At the proper time, a brahmin seeking merit who would sacrifice should offer the sacrificial oblation to them—
those who are free from greed, without the sense of "mine," and devoid of desire.
Their taints are destroyed and they have lived the holy life;
at the proper time, a brahmin seeking merit should offer oblations to them when they sacrifice.
Those indeed who have not fallen into the snares of craving,
who move about free from possessiveness— they shall cross over the flood.
One should offer sacrificial food to them at the proper time.
That brahmin who, seeking merit, should sacrifice—
yet for whom there is no craving anywhere in the world for becoming or non-becoming, either here or in the hereafter;
At the proper time, a Brahmin seeking merit who would sacrifice should offer the sacrificial oblation to them— those who,
having abandoned sensual pleasures, wander as householders.
Straight as a shuttle because of his self-restraint,
a brahmin who seeks merit and desires to sacrifice should offer the sacrificial oblation to them at the proper time.
To those who are free from passion, whose faculties are well-composed,
like the moon released from the grasp of Rāhu—
to them one should offer the sacrificial oblation at the proper time.
That brahmin who, seeking merit, should sacrifice to those who have stilled [the defilements],
who are free from passion and free from anger,
for whom there is no further destination here once they have cast off [the body];
At the proper time, a brahmin seeking merit who would sacrifice should offer the sacrificial oblation to them; thus,
having abandoned birth and death without remainder, he shall attain the state beyond all suffering.
A brahmin seeking merit who would sacrifice should offer the sacrificial oblation to them at the proper time— those who have transcended all doubt.
To those who wander in the world with themselves as their island,
possessing nothing and liberated in every respect—
to them one should offer sacrificial food at the proper time.
That brahmin who, seeking merit, should sacrifice—those here who know this as it truly is:
"This is the last birth; there is no further becoming."
At the proper time, a Brahmin seeking merit who would sacrifice should offer the sacrificial oblation to them;
he who is a master of the Vedas, delighting in meditation, and possessed of mindfulness.
He who has attained full enlightenment is a refuge for many;
at the proper time, a brahmin seeking merit should offer oblations to him when he performs a sacrifice.
“Surely my questioning was not in vain,” thought the young brahmin Māgha,
“for the Blessed One has explained to me those worthy of offerings.”
You know this matter here exactly as it is,
for this Dhamma is known to you:
that the householder who is a lord of giving is devoted to making requests.
One who desires merit, seeking merit,
gives food and drink here to others;
tell me, Blessed One, the perfection of sacrifice.
“Sacrifice as a sacrificer,
Māgha,” said the Blessed One,
“and let your mind be serene in every respect.”
The object is the sacrifice for the sacrificer;
by establishing himself therein, he abandons hatred.
Free from passion, he should likewise dispel hatred.
Cultivating a boundless mind of loving-kindness,
being constantly heedful day and night,
he pervades all directions with this immeasurable state.
“Who is purified, who is liberated, and who is bound?
By what means does one go to the Brahma-world?
O Sage, being asked by me who do not know, please explain.”
The Blessed One is indeed my witness, seen as the origin of the Brahma-world;
for you are equal to Brahmā for us, this is the truth.
How does one who is radiant attain the Brahma-world?
“Whoever performs the threefold perfection of sacrifice,
O Māgha,” said the Blessed One,
“such a person, being like-minded, wins over those worthy of offerings.”
“Having sacrificed thus, being devoted to right giving, one is reborn in the Brahma-world; so I say.
When this was said, the young brahmin Māgha said this to the Blessed One:
“Excellent, Master Gotama!
… [as before] … From this day forth, for as long as life shall last, we go for refuge to him.
The Māgha Sutta, the fifth.
